The Poison Squad was a group of young male volunteers who ate food laced with chemical preservatives in a United States government experiment, from 1902 to 1904. It was run by the chemist Harvey Washington Wiley, head of the Department of Agriculture's Bureau of Chemistry.

Wiley wanted to learn whether additives such as borax, formaldehyde and salicylic acid harmed human health. Twelve men at a time ate meals at a "hygienic table" in Washington, with the dose increased in steps and their health checked closely. The press named them the Poison Squad. None died, but some fell ill, which gave Wiley evidence of harm.

The newspaper coverage made food safety a public issue. This work helped build support for the Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906.
